chunks.text: Ficus benghalensis, the banyan, is India's national tree and an evergreen, fast-growing strangler fig native to the Indian subcontinent, capable of reaching 30 m in height but more often spreading sideways far beyond its height through a distinctive growth habit: aerial roots descend from its branches, root in the soil below, and thicken into secondary trunks that let a single tree expand into what looks like a small forest. It typically begins life as an epiphyte on a host tree, which it eventually envelops and can outcompete — the origin of the 'strangler fig' name. Its figs are dispersed by birds such as the Indian myna and coppersmith barbet, whose digestion aids germination; in Hawaii, where it has been introduced but lacks its specific pollinating wasp, it grows well in cultivation but has never naturalised beyond planted specimens. Religiously, it is sacred across all three of India's major indigenous traditions: Hindu temples are frequently built near banyan trees, Theravada Buddhists associate it with the enlightenment of the twenty-fourth Buddha, Kassapa, and Jain tradition holds that the first Tirthankara, Adinatha, attained spiritual enlightenment beneath one. India hosts several famous giant specimens by canopy area, led by Thimmamma Marrimanu in Andhra Pradesh (about 19,107 sq m, also the largest tree perimeter on record at roughly 846 m) and the Great Banyan in Kolkata's botanic garden (about 18,918 sq m).

The Great Banyan, growing in the Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden at Shibpur, Howrah, near Kolkata, is probably the single most famous individual banyan tree in the world and was recorded as the largest tree specimen on Earth in the 1989 Guinness Book of World Records. Believed to be at least 250 years old (one source cited on the page puts it at 270), it today covers roughly 18,918 sq m via 3,772 aerial prop roots, with its highest branch reaching about 24.5 m — it now resembles a dense grove more than a single tree, encircled by a 330 m path that the canopy has already outgrown. Its most striking feature is that it has no visible main trunk at all: the original trunk, about 15.25 m in diameter, was progressively weakened by fungal infection after cyclone damage and was deliberately removed in 1925 to keep the rest of the tree healthy, leaving only a small, hard-to-reach memorial marker at the tree's historic centre. Sources are inconsistent about exactly which storms caused the damage — cyclones are variously dated to 1864 and 1867, or to 1884 and 1886 in other accounts — so the precise dates should be treated as unresolved, though it is well documented that Cyclone Amphan in May 2020 destroyed several of the tree's prop roots and broke some main branches, and that the tree nonetheless survives and continues spreading outward today.
